items.title: Adolphe Alexander Interview, 1961-03-08
items.q: His father died. I saw him in California.

ctx.x: Maurice Duran. Maurice Duran. Maurice Duran used to play with my, well, Maurice Duran used to have, him and Willie Humphries have a band together. Duran and Humphrey, when I was playing with Celestan and Rizley. Duran and Humphrey. Celestan and Rizley. Yeah. A lot of times we used to play with two bands. Yeah, Celestan and Humphrey. But after that, when I joined, when I joined, when I joined, uh, Ma'am Perez, Maurice Duran was playing with Ma'am Perez. Second trumpet. Yeah. He's not playing. He's not playing at…
time ago. His father died. I saw him in California. I know him. You met him? Yeah. Two years ago, I saw him. Yeah. He was a good trumpet player. Yeah.

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Adolphe Alexander played the [expletive deleted] out the clarinet, but he never was featured. Hell of a musician.

ctx.x: . . . with a gun and stuff, and he smashed . . . All the musicians ran. Jumped out the window, and he smashed all the instruments. Bunk’s trumpet was on the chair or something, and it got smashed up. Let me ask you this, Mr. Barker. You . . . Who were some of the better that you heard in New Orleans before you, before the ’20s, before you were a kid? Like some of the better clarinet players and trombone players.

There was a gang of them. Adolphe Alexander played the [expletive deleted] out the clarinet, but he never was featured. Hell of a musician. There was Alexander’s family. He had two brothers. One played drums. One played piano. The old man played baritone horn with my grandfather in the Onward Brass Band. There was Chris Kelly, a great trumpet player. It was funky. Had a following. A lot of people liked his music. At night he played a funky blues, nine different blues in nine different tempos. He played yard…
Did he end up playing bass?
